newsitem.title: USA: Dlr tumbles at US close after Fed holds rates firm.
newsitem.headline: Dlr tumbles at US close after Fed holds rates firm.

text.p: The dollar tumbled against most major currencies on Tuesday after Federal Reserve policymakers held rates steady, disappointing dollar bulls who had hoped for tighter credit.
The magnitude of the dollar's slide surprised foreign exchange dealers and could mark the end of the dollar's impressive two-year rise against the mark and yen, dealers said.
"We're looking at the possibility of higher rates in Japan and this certainly doesn't help the dollar's overall trend (higher)," said Mellon Bank's Kevin Lawrie.
"It may confirm the end of that trend," Lawrie, global manager of foreign exchange, added.
Trade was fast and furious after the central bank policy-setting meeting disbanded mid-afternoon with no official rate announcement -- a signal official interest rates remain unchanged.
"The dollar is getting hit. We are going down hard," said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, as the dollar began its slide through layers of critical supports.

By the U.S. close, the dollar had fallen more than two pfennigs to 1.6765/75 marks from 1.6970/80 at the open and shed a yen to 112.58/68 from 113.60/70 at the open and three yen from 115.57/62 at Monday's close.
The dollar also slipped against the Swiss franc to 1.3860/70 from 1.4065/75 at the start of U.S. trade.

Polls prior to the Fed meeting showed Wall Street was almost equally divided on whether the Fed would raise rates to corral any inflationary pressures. However, dealers said given the currency market's decisive reaction to the news of steady rates, the bias must have been for a rise in rates.
"I thought the market was pretty evenly divided on this, but the fact is the market is following the path of least resistance," said David Gilmore, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.

Against the yen, the dollar has been on a downward spiral ever since hitting a 56-month high of 127.47 yen on May 1. In overseas trade, the dollar fell below 112 yen to its lowest level since December at 111.98 yen after news reports hinted at prospects for higher interest rates in Japan.

Japanese media reported that Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party would recommend later this month that the Bank of Japan raise its offical discount rate from a current record-low 0.5 percent to keep capital from flowing out of the country following the liberalization of trade laws.
Japanese finance authorities moved to halt the ensuing steep slide in the dollar, warning that the yen's rise was too rapid.
"The pace of the yen's strengthening is too rapid," Eisuke Sakakibara, the director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau told Reuters.
Sakakibara added that too much volatility in foreign exchange markets was undesirable and that Japan would "deal appropriately" with such excessive volatility.
His remarks helped push the dollar back above 113 yen before news of steady U.S. rates sent the dollar tumbling once again.
Gilmore said market talk of higher interest rates in Japan was "more of an excuse to sell dollars than a reflection of economic reality".

In other trading, sterling jumped to $1.6560/70 from $1.6437/47 and the dollar dipped to Canadian $1.3667/72 from C$1.3725/30. The Australian dollar closed higher at $0.7739/44 from $0.7723/28 at the open.
